prize_parts.citation: for the optical lattice clock, based on magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms, and its realisation at the 10^-18 level of fractional uncertainty

statement.case_for: I keep B036 with Katori and Ye as a single prize part. The round-1 exchange sharpened rather than weakened the case. The discovery-or-invention test, as I understand it, asks who originated the work and what the specific act was. Here the answer is unusually short: Katori proposed magic-wavelength trapping, which removes the light shift of the clock transition while thousands of atoms are interrogated in parallel, and Ye's group took the strontium lattice clock into the 10^-18 regime by controlling systematics, coherence and many-body effects. The result has been reproduced with Sr, Yb and Hg in several laboratories and compared across links, so its interpretation is not in question, which cannot yet be said for the central open question in magic-angle graphene. Kroll's and Lindroth's drafts converge with mine on a citation drawn around the lattice concept and its 10^-18 realisation, which also answers the overlap objection by claiming nothing about optical timekeeping in general or about lattice versus ion clocks. On the chair's drafting question, my sentence is the one in the citation field, and it leaves ion clocks, the comb lineage and other lattice-clock groups outside the claim by naming only the neutral-atom lattice concept. I would leave Ye's many-body and spin-exchange work out of the wording, though it is part of why his group reached the record regime. I treat opening support counts as a signal to test, not as merit, and the test here has been passed on the science.
statement.case_against: The objection I take most seriously is Eriksson's, shared by Danielsson and Mehlig in different words: that this is a precision advance, 'another digit', built on tools honoured in 2005 (the frequency comb) and 2012 (control of single quantum systems and ion clocks), not a new phenomenon. I do not think that objection is empty. My answer is that the magic-wavelength lattice is a distinct conceptual step with its own physics, but it is a judgement about novelty and I cannot prove it with evidence. The second weakness is credit. Lemonde, Gill, Takamoto, the PTB, NIST and SYRTE groups, and the Ye-group contributors have close claims, and two names cannot capture all of them. Third, the pending redefinition of the second has not happened, and I would not want the committee's timing to be tied to a metrology decision either way. Finally, the scientific case for B022 is stronger than my own colleagues in the B036 group have always conceded, and if the pairing question settles in the next few years that comparison will look different.

responses.point: Danielsson maintains that B022 is early but defensible: the phenomena are reproduced across many devices and platforms, the open question is the pairing mechanism rather than the existence of the effects, and a prize for a new phenomenon should weigh above a precision refinement.
responses.response: I accept the reproduction point and I have ranked B022 third and keep it as my first alternative. Where I still part from you is the criterion. Mehlig's framing, that the prize would rest on flat-band-driven correlated phases and not on a theory of superconductivity, is the best version of your case, but the citation as you wrote it names superconducting states, and those are exactly where the interpretation is unsettled and sample-to-sample twist-angle disorder is a real obstacle. The credit gap, with Yuan Cao outside the three names, is not repaired by the wording you propose. If Cao's omission and the earlier moire-theory contributors can be answered, and the mechanism question narrows, I would move B022 up for a later year. This year I do not think those conditions are met, and I would not accept that timing alone is a reason to prefer the less mature result.

responses.point: Eriksson says he would take B036 as a serious configuration if Kroll and Lindroth could show the magic-wavelength idea is the decisive conceptual step, and that novelty relative to 2005 and 2012 is his remaining reservation.
responses.response: Since you invited the clock people to answer this, I will try from the instrument side. The 2005 comb is a way of counting optical cycles and the 2012 prize is about manipulating and measuring single quantum systems. Neither addresses the obstacle that Katori's proposal removes: that a trapping light field shifts the clock transition, so an atom array cannot be held without ruining the frequency. Choosing the wavelength at which the two clock states are shifted equally is the idea, and it is what makes a million-atom measurement possible. I would call that a distinct invention, though I agree it is a judgement and not a measurement. I also do not think your B054 case fails; it is my fourth-ranked candidate and I have listed it as an alternative, but the omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang is a credit gap I cannot see how to close.

responses.point: Kroll proposes a citation framed around the lattice concept so that it does not adjudicate lattice versus ion clocks, and he flags his research stay in John Hall's laboratory as a possible recusal question for B036.
responses.response: I agree with the framing and I have used it. On the recusal I would say two things. A doctoral research stay in a laboratory whose lineage is linked to Ye's group is a documented scientific connection, not a collaboration with the credited names, and by his own account he has no tie to Katori or Ye. My own view is that this is a matter for acquaintance-level disclosure, and I would not ask him to withdraw, but the committee should record the disclosure and decide it openly. Because B036 has four explicit supporters who do not share that history, I do not believe his abstention would change the outcome.

responses.point: Lindroth would include Ye's many-body and spin-exchange control among the credited contributions that made 10^-18 reachable, and she lists Lemonde, Gill, Takamoto and the Ludlow, Hinkley and Bloom contributors as sharing credit at the margin.
responses.response: I take the physics point, since the control of collisions and spin exchange is a real part of why the record was achieved. My preference is still to keep it out of the citation, because a second storyline invites the committee to weigh Ye's whole programme, including thorium and other work, and that dilutes a clean claim. I think the right solution is to have the citation say 'its realisation at the 10^-18 level', which covers the many-body control implicitly without naming it. The marginal names you list are the real cost of a two-name prize and I do not dispute that. I would answer them by saying that this prize honours a concept and its first record-level realisation, not every contributor, and that the citation should say so.

responses.point: Johansson prefers B046, optical-lattice quantum simulation, as a field with two decades of replication, but accepts that it may be a method and not a discovery and that three names exclude Cirac, Esslinger and Jaksch.
responses.response: I take the maturity and replication point seriously; the Mott transition and gas microscopy are real discoveries about interacting lattices. My difficulty is the same one you name yourself: the choice of three from five or six names would be a decisive injustice to whoever is left out, and the question of whether simulation is a discovery or a method is open. B036 has a cleaner two-name map to two contributions. I would not describe the clock as having broader scientific reach than quantum simulation, but the credit allocation is clearer, and that matters for a prize that has to name individuals.

uncertainties: Whether the committee is persuaded that the magic-wavelength lattice is a distinct invention from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes. That is a judgement about novelty and I cannot settle it by evidence.
Whether a two-name prize that leaves out Lemonde, Gill, Takamoto and the national-laboratory groups can be defended, and whether the citation wording is narrow enough to carry that.
Whether the pairing mechanism and interpretation in magic-angle graphene will clarify within a few years, which would change my view of B022 for a later cycle.
I recall the history of the clock field from general knowledge and have not independently verified the details of priority between the Katori and Ye groups.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure. My preferred configuration, B036 (Katori, Ye), is outside my own microscopy and materials field, and I report no specific conflict with either name from the provided profile. B021 (aberration correction), which I ranked first at the opening, is my own field and I may know its candidates through the microscopy community and the International Federation of Societies for Microscopy; I no longer support it in my configuration, and I would recuse myself from any decision on it if the ties proved closer than acquaintance. I have dropped it from my alternatives for that reason and because no other member supports it. On the question raised for Kroll, I have no information beyond what he reports and I would treat his Hall-laboratory connection as an open disclosure for the committee to decide. My Chalmers colleague Goran Johansson now supports B046, with which I have no connection.
